fetched_contents.text: A Review of Filtration Performance of Protective Masks Abstract Masks are essential and effective small protective devices used to protect the general public against infections such as COVID-19. However, available systematic reviews and summaries on the filtration performance of masks are lacking. Therefore, in order to investigate the filtration performance of masks, filtration mechanisms, mask characteristics, and the relationships between influencing factors and protective performance were first analyzed through mask evaluations. The summary of filtration mechanisms and mask characteristics provides readers with a clear and easy-to-understand theoretical cognition. Then, a detailed analysis of influencing factors and the relationships between the influencing factors and filtration performance is presented in. The influence of the aerosol size and type on filtration performance is nonlinear and nonconstant, and filtration efficiency decreases with an increase in the gas flow rate; moreover, fitness plays a decisive role in the protective effects of masks. It is recommended that the public should wear surgical masks to prevent COVID-19 infection in low-risk and non-densely populated areas. Future research should focus on fitness tests, and the formulation of standards should also be accelerated. This paper provides a systematic review that will be helpful for the design of masks and public health in the future. Keywords: personal protective equipment, masks, filtration efficiency, overall protective performance 1. Introduction We are currently living in an environment where viruses and bacteria are everywhere; however, masks can protect people from being infected by viruses and bacteria as an effective means of physical prevention [1,2]. Some examples of viral outbreaks include the SARS virus, which broke out in 2003, the Middle East Respiratory Syndrome coronavirus, which was discovered in 2012, and the largest Ebola virus outbreak in the years 2014–2016. Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus Type 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and its variants have continued to ravage the world since 2020 due to their high transmissibility and high global death rate [3,4,5]. Health management remains an extremely important topic worldwide. Masks as a basic means of protection have been shown to aid in protecting people’s lives. The virus is transmitted through air-borne droplets or spray, which have been identified as the major routes for cross-infection with coronavirus 2019 (COVID-19) among human populations [5]. The function of a mask is to stop the spread of the virus, which attaches to aerosol airborne particles or respiratory fluid droplets. The evidence shows that it is useful for healthy people to wear masks in the community during a pandemic [6,7,8]. Wearing respirators at work is an effective way to avoid infection and death in healthcare workers [6,7,8,9], and hospital staff have been instructed to change their masks every two hours when conditions permit [9]. Airborne transmission of respiratory viruses is divided into exhalation, transport, and inhalation [10]. It recommended that HCWs wear medical masks when in contact with an infected person and cover their noses and mouths during coughing or sneezing with either a tissue or a flexed elbow [10]; otherwise, exhaled virions would continue to circulate in the air 10 s later without wearing a mask. Because the virus is deposited in aerosols and transmitted via speaking, coughing, or sneezing, a comprehensive understanding of the evolution of respiratory droplets is necessary to determine the transmission mechanisms of respiratory diseases [11]. Therefore, masks play a very important role in health management and future outbreaks of novel viruses [12]. Filtration efficiency is the most critical factor in the protective performance of masks, but the development of mask materials is the key to determining filtration efficiency. The materials used for masks are being continuously developed. Gauze masks were the earliest mask materials; early surgical masks mostly comprised 8 to 12 layers of cotton yarn [13]. The multi-layer dense accumulation of cotton yarn makes the fibers show a cross-pore structure, which can physically intercept larger particles or dust in the air. Cotton yarn also easily absorbs moisture, and the blocking efficiency is low [14]. In the 1960s, non-woven mask technology was born, and disposable masks were developed during the same period [15]. The masks are made using the melt-blowing technique, a process in which electrical charges are injected into the material, creating a quasi-permanent electric field that provides sufficient particulate matter (PM) filtration through an electrostatic force [16]. Non-woven fibrous substances such as polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE), polylactic acid (PLA), and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) are the most studied materials [16,17,18]. Polypropylene melt-blown nonwoven fibers have stable properties, a fine fiber diameter (0.5–4 μm), high porosity, good air permeability, and good filtration resistance; therefore, the performance of the filter material prepared using polypropylene is much better than that of other materials [17,18]. Furthermore, studies have demonstrated that the electret filter (non-woven fibers) has a higher filtration efficiency, lower air resistance, and greater dust-holding capacity compared with traditional fiber filters [18,19]. Polypropylene nonwovens can also be electrized to give the fibers an electrical charge. The filtration efficiency of polypropylene non-woven fibers regarding dust, air bubbles, and viruses can reach 98.9%, and the filtration resistance is only 37.92 Pa under the effect of coulomb adsorption [18]. For masks, the research objectives have always included achieving a larger capacity, optimal comfort, efficient elimination of biological aerosols, and optimal filtering of air particles [20]. fetched_contents.text: Masks and Respiratory Viruses Prevention | Respiratory Illnesses * Wearing a mask is an additional prevention strategy that offers you an extra layer of protection from respiratory illness. * This action can be helpful in certain settings, like crowded spaces or when illnesses are increasing in your community, or if you or someone you spend time with is at higher risk of getting very sick. An additional strategy to further protect yourself and others Wearing a mask can help lower the risk of respiratory virus transmission. When worn by a person with an infection, masks reduce the spread of the virus to others. Masks can also protect wearers from breathing in infectious particles from people around them. Different masks offer different levels of protection. Wearing the most protective one you can comfortably wear for extended periods of time that fits well (completely covering the nose and mouth) is the most effective option. How it works Generally, masks can help act as a filter to reduce the number of germs you breathe in or out. Their effectiveness can vary against different viruses, for example, based on the size of the virus. When worn by a person who has a virus, masks can reduce the chances they spread it to others. Masks can also protect wearers from inhaling germs; this type of protection typically comes from better fitting masks (for example, N95 or KN95 respirators). There are many different types of masks, and how well they block viruses depends on their design and how well they fit against your face. Cloth masks generally offer lower levels of protection to wearers, surgical/disposable masks usually offer more protection, international filtering facepiece respirators (like KN95 respirators) offer even more, and the most protective respirators are NIOSH Approved® filtering facepiece respirators (like N95® respirators). Steps you can take * When choosing to wear a mask, choose the most protective type you can. * Determine how well it fits. Gaps can let air leak in and out. Check for gaps by cupping your hands around the outside edges of the mask. If the mask has a good fit, you will feel warm air come through the front of the mask and may be able to see the mask material move in and out with each breath. * Learn about proper technique for wearing an N95 respirator. Steps organizations can take Provide free, high-quality masks to your workforce or visitors in times of higher respiratory viral spread. Key times for prevention All of the prevention strategies can be helpful to reduce risk. Additional measures, like wearing a mask, are especially helpful when: * Respiratory viruses are causing a lot of illness in your community. * You or the people around you were recently exposed to a respiratory virus, are sick, or are recovering. * You or the people around you have risk factors for severe illness. # Effectiveness comparison of surgical masks and N95 respirators

## Filtration efficiency and particle capture for bacterial-sized aerosols

The evidence strongly suggests that N95 respirators are designed to provide more particle filtration than surgical masks. A review on filtration performance states that N95 respirators are intended to achieve a very close facial fit and very efficient filtration of airborne particles, and that the edges are designed to form a seal around the nose and mouth [N5-F3]. Another source notes that surgical masks may not provide the expected protection level against small virions and that some surgical masks may let a significant amount of air through [N1-R4]. A study on filtration performance of protective masks similarly says that the mask material tested at 0.3 mm had particle filtration more than 95%, and that N95 masks were certified in that context [N1-R1]. A separate study on particle filtration efficiency of respirators during the COVID-19 pandemic found that total particle penetration for N95 respirators ranged from 2.5% to 5.5%, depending on conditions [N1-R2]. In contrast, the same review says that surgical masks may also provide more protection than cloth masks, but it also emphasizes that surgical masks are not regulated for particulate filtration efficiency and do not provide complete protection because of loose fit [N5-F3]. A study on aerosol penetration through surgical masks tested two surgical masks at a wide particle size range [N1-R3], which implies that surgical masks are evaluated for particle capture, but the evidence here does not give a direct comparable efficiency figure for bacterial-sized aerosols. Overall, the direct evidence supports N95 respirators as more efficient at capturing airborne particles than surgical masks, especially for smaller particles where N95s are certified for close-fitting filtration [N5-F3][N1-R1][N1-R2].

## Leakage and fit-related protection differences

Fit is a major determinant of protection. The review explicitly states that fitness plays a decisive role in the protective effects of masks [N1-F1]. The CDC guidance says that better-fitting masks, such as N95 respirators, can protect wearers from inhaling germs because of the close facial fit [N5-F2]. The same guidance also says that surgical masks are not intended to form a seal around the nose and mouth and may not filter or block very small particles in the air [N5-F3]. The evidence on fit leakage is indirect but still important: a study on surgical masks over N95 respirators warns that covering an N95 respirator with a surgical mask can increase face-to-mask seal leakage [N2-R1]. Another study on the effect of wearing a surgical mask over an N95 respirator found that the breathing resistance was affected by this combination [N2-R3]. A study comparing inward leakage rates between N95 respirators and modified surgical masks also found differences in fit performance [N2-R4][N2-R5]. Taken together, these sources show that surgical masks are inherently more leak-prone because they do not form a seal, whereas N95 respirators are designed to reduce leakage through a close facial fit [N5-F3][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5].

## Settings where one mask type is more effective than the other

The evidence points to setting-specific tradeoffs. In high-risk, close-contact settings where airborne transmission is likely, N95 respirators are more effective because they combine higher filtration efficiency with a better fit [N5-F2][N5-F3]. The CDC guidance specifically recommends that people wear the most protective mask they can comfortably wear for extended periods that fits well [N5-F2]. In contrast, surgical masks are more appropriate for situations where barrier protection against large droplets and splashes is the main concern, rather than for filtering small airborne particles [N5-F3]. The review also states that surgical masks may be effective in blocking splashes and large-particle droplets, but they do not filter or block very small particles in the air [N5-F3]. In settings with heavy exposure to infectious aerosols, such as healthcare environments or crowded indoor spaces, the evidence supports N95 respirators as the more effective choice [N5-F2][N5-F3]. In settings where comfort and prolonged wear are important, surgical masks may be preferred because they are generally easier to tolerate, but this can come at the cost of reduced protection [N5-F2][N5-F3].

## Bottom line

For bacterial-sized aerosols, the evidence suggests that N95 respirators are more effective than surgical masks because they are designed for close-fitting filtration and have lower penetration rates for airborne particles [N5-F3][N1-R1][N1-R2]. Surgical masks are less effective because they do not form a seal and are not regulated for particulate filtration efficiency [N5-F3]. Fit and leakage differences are central to the protection gap: N95 respirators reduce inward leakage through a seal, whereas surgical masks depend on a loose fit and are more leak-prone [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The best settings for N95s are high-risk, close-contact, or aerosol-rich environments, while surgical masks are better suited to lower-risk settings where barrier protection against droplets is the main need [N5-F2][N5-F3].

# Comfort and compliance comparison of surgical masks and N95 respirators

## Breathing resistance, heat, humidity, and face pressure

Comfort is a major factor in mask use. The evidence on fit-related leakage suggests that surgical masks can increase breathing resistance when worn over an N95 respirator [N2-R3]. Although the cited excerpt does not give numerical values, it implies that mask layering or fit changes can affect breathing resistance. The CDC guidance also notes that masks should be worn in a way that fits well and that gaps can let air leak in and out, which is relevant to comfort because poor fit can make a mask feel less comfortable and harder to breathe through [N5-F2]. The review on filtration performance emphasizes that fitness plays a decisive role in protective effects and that comfort and optimal elimination of biological aerosols are important mask design objectives [N1-F1]. While the evidence here does not provide direct measurements of heat, humidity, or face pressure, it supports the general principle that mask comfort is tied to fit, breathing resistance, and ease of use [N1-F1][N5-F2][N2-R3].

## User acceptance, mask fit, and mask-changing behavior

User acceptance is closely linked to mask fit and comfort. The CDC guidance specifically recommends choosing the most protective mask that fits well and can be comfortably worn for extended periods [N5-F2]. It also advises checking for gaps and determining whether the mask fits by feeling warm air coming through the front or seeing the material move with each breath [N5-F2]. The evidence on surgical masks over N95s warns that covering an N95 with a surgical mask can increase seal leakage, which is likely to reduce user acceptance because it may feel less secure or less effective [N2-R1]. A study on compliance with face mask use during the COVID-19 pandemic found that surgical mask use was associated with improved compliance compared to fabric masks [N4-R3]. This suggests that surgical masks may be more accepted in some populations because they are less restrictive than respirators, but the study does not directly compare surgical masks to N95s. The CDC guidance also says that masks should be changed when damaged, soiled, or when breathing becomes difficult [N5-F3]. Taken together, the evidence indicates that surgical masks are generally more accepted in daily use because they are easier to wear, but N95s may be less accepted if users perceive them as uncomfortable or hard to fit [N5-F2][N5-F3][N4-R3].

## How comfort affects prolonged use and real-world adherence

Comfort is a key determinant of prolonged use and real-world adherence. The CDC guidance emphasizes that the most effective option is the mask that is the most protective and fits well, and that comfort matters because people are more likely to wear masks consistently when they are comfortable [N5-F2]. The same guidance notes that masks should be worn for extended periods and that fit is important because gaps can let air leak in and out [N5-F2]. A study on prolonged mask use found that long-term face mask use can affect physiological and psychological problems, which reinforces the importance of comfort in sustained wear [N4-R1]. The evidence also shows that mask-changing behavior is tied to comfort: surgical masks should be discarded when breathing becomes difficult, and users are expected to replace masks when they are damaged or soiled [N5-F3]. In real-world use, comfort affects adherence because masks that are uncomfortable, hot, or difficult to breathe through are less likely to be worn consistently [N5-F2][N4-R1][N5-F3]. Therefore, while N95 respirators offer greater protection, their comfort tradeoffs can reduce adherence, whereas surgical masks may be more widely used in everyday settings but offer less protection [N5-F2][N5-F3][N4-R1].

# Bacterial aerosol behavior and transmission context for mask comparison

## Typical size range and persistence of airborne bacterial pathogens

The evidence on aerosolized pathogen transmission indicates that airborne pathogens can exist as droplet nuclei and can remain airborne for variable times depending on particle size. A review on the role of particle size in aerosolized pathogen transmission notes that particle size is central to understanding infectious disease spread [N6-R1]. Another review similarly emphasizes that particle size determines the behavior of infectious aerosols [N6-R3]. A study on particle sizes of infectious aerosols states that airborne transmission is often attributed to infectious droplet nuclei produced by the desiccation of suspended droplets, defined as 5 µm or smaller [N6-R4]. A separate source says that the size of particles (0.001 to >100 µm) allows them to remain airborne for a variable amount of time and that infectious aerosols contain pathogens [N6-R5]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that airborne bacterial pathogens span a wide size range, but the most concerning transmissible particles are typically smaller, especially droplet nuclei in the 5 µm or smaller range [N6-R4][N6-R5]. Smaller particles are more persistent in the air and more likely to be inhaled, which makes them more difficult to block with masks that do not provide close-fitting filtration [N6-R4][N6-R5].

## Differences between droplet, aerosol, and airborne transmission

The evidence distinguishes transmission routes by particle behavior. Droplet transmission involves larger particles that settle more quickly, whereas airborne transmission involves smaller particles that remain suspended longer [N6-R4][N6-R5]. A review on aerosol-mediated disease transmission describes an interdisciplinary approach combining aerosol physics, surface chemistry, and biology to understand airborne pathogen transmission [N6-R2]. The CDC guidance on respiratory viruses also notes that masks can reduce the spread of virus from an infected person and can protect wearers from inhaling infectious particles [N5-F2]. In this context, droplet transmission is more localized and short-range, while airborne transmission is more persistent and can spread further [N6-R4][N6-R5]. The evidence does not directly separate bacterial from viral aerosols, but it does show that mask effectiveness depends on the particle size range and how long the pathogen remains airborne [N6-R4][N6-R5].

## How transmission mode affects mask effectiveness

Mask effectiveness is therefore highly dependent on the transmission mode. For droplet transmission, surgical masks may be more useful because they can block large droplets and splashes [N5-F3]. For airborne transmission, especially with smaller droplet nuclei, N95 respirators are more effective because they are designed for close-fitting filtration and can reduce inward leakage [N5-F3][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The CDC guidance also states that better-fitting masks, such as N95 respirators, can protect wearers from inhaling germs [N5-F2]. A study on mask use to avoid airborne contamination during COVID-19 suggests that masks can reduce the distance airborne pathogens travel [N3-R5], which supports the idea that mask fit and filtration reduce exposure in airborne settings [N3-R5]. In short, masks are less effective against larger droplets than against smaller airborne particles, and the evidence supports using N95 respirators for airborne transmission risks while surgical masks are more suitable for droplet-based or lower-risk settings [N5-F3][N5-F2][N6-R4][N6-R5].

# Limitations and context-specific tradeoffs in mask selection

## Assumptions about aerosol generation and exposure levels

The evidence shows that mask effectiveness depends heavily on the assumptions about aerosol generation and exposure levels. The CDC guidance notes that masks should be worn in settings where respiratory viruses are causing a lot of illness, or when individuals are at higher risk of severe illness [N5-F2]. It also emphasizes that the optimal way to prevent transmission is to use a combination of interventions, not just PPE alone [N5-F3]. The filtration review says that filtration efficiency decreases with increasing gas flow rate and that fitness plays a decisive role in protective effects [N1-F1]. This means that mask effectiveness is not static: it depends on how much people breathe, how tightly the mask fits, and how much aerosol is present in the environment. The evidence also suggests that N95 respirators are more effective than surgical masks, but only when fit is good and exposure levels are high enough to justify their use [N1-F1][N5-F3].

## Relevance of bacterial vs viral transmission evidence

The evidence provided is more directly about viral respiratory pathogens than bacterial aerosols, but it still informs bacterial comparisons. The CDC guidance states that masks can protect wearers from inhaling germs and that better-fitting masks, such as N95 respirators, offer more protection [N5-F2]. The evidence highlights several practical constraints. The CDC guidance notes that mask selection should balance protection with comfort and fit, and that people should wear the most protective mask they can comfortably wear for extended periods [N5-F2]. It also says that masks should be changed when damaged, soiled, or when breathing becomes difficult [N5-F3]. This implies that availability and replacement frequency matter in real-world use. A study on prolonged mask use found that long-term face mask use can affect physiological and psychological problems, which reinforces the importance of comfort and practicality [N4-R1]. Overall, the evidence supports a context-specific tradeoff: N95 respirators are more effective for high-risk settings, but they may be less available, more expensive, and harder to tolerate than surgical masks [N5-F2][N5-F3][N4-R1].

In high-risk, close-contact settings where airborne transmission is likely, N95 respirators are more effective because they combine higher filtration efficiency with better fit and lower leakage [N5-F2][N5-F3]. The CDC guidance specifically recommends that people wear the most protective mask they can comfortably wear for extended periods that fits well [N5-F2]. In contrast, surgical masks are more appropriate for situations where barrier protection against large droplets and splashes is the main concern, rather than for filtering small airborne particles [N5-F3]. The review also states that surgical masks may be effective in blocking splashes and large-particle droplets, but they do not filter or block very small particles in the air [N5-F3]. In settings with heavy exposure to infectious aerosols, such as healthcare environments or crowded indoor spaces, the evidence supports N95 respirators as the more effective choice [N5-F2][N5-F3].

In lower-risk settings where comfort and prolonged wear are important, surgical masks may be preferred because they are generally easier to tolerate [N5-F2][N5-F3]. The CDC guidance also notes that masks should be changed when damaged, soiled, or when breathing becomes difficult [N5-F3]. This means that surgical masks may be more suitable for everyday use where the risk of airborne transmission is lower and the need for frequent replacement is manageable [N5-F2][N5-F3]. Overall, the best settings for N95 respirators are high-risk, close-contact, or aerosol-rich environments, while surgical masks are better suited to lower-risk settings where barrier protection against droplets is the main need [N5-F2][N5-F3].

## 5) Limitations and tradeoffs in real-world use

The evidence highlights several limitations and tradeoffs. Mask effectiveness depends heavily on assumptions about aerosol generation and exposure levels [N5-F2][N1-F1]. The CDC guidance notes that masks should be worn in settings where respiratory viruses are causing a lot of illness, or when individuals are at higher risk of severe illness [N5-F2]. It also emphasizes that the optimal way to prevent transmission is to use a combination of interventions, not just PPE alone [N5-F3]. The filtration review says that filtration efficiency decreases with increasing gas flow rate and that fitness plays a decisive role in protective effects [N1-F1]. This means mask effectiveness is not static: it depends on how much people breathe, how tightly the mask fits, and how much aerosol is present in the environment.

The evidence provided is more directly about viral respiratory pathogens than bacterial aerosols, but it still informs bacterial comparisons. The CDC guidance states that masks can protect wearers from inhaling germs and that better-fitting masks, such as N95 respirators, offer more protection [N5-F2]. The FDA page explicitly says that surgical masks are not intended to provide complete protection from germs and that N95 respirators provide respiratory protection to the wearer [N5-F3]. A review on filtration performance notes that masks are essential for protecting against infections such as COVID-19 and that airborne transmission involves exhalation, transport, and inhalation [N1-F1]. While the evidence here does not specifically quantify bacterial transmission, it supports the general principle that N95 respirators are more protective than surgical masks against airborne pathogens, which includes bacterial aerosols [N1-F1][N5-F2][N5-F3]. However, the evidence is weaker for bacteria-specific comparisons because the studies are framed around respiratory viruses, not bacteria [N5-F3].

Cost, availability, and practical constraints also matter in real-world use. The CDC guidance notes that mask selection should balance protection with comfort and fit, and that people should wear the most protective mask they can comfortably wear for extended periods [N5-F2]. It also says that masks should be changed when damaged, soiled, or when breathing becomes difficult [N5-F3]. This implies that availability and replacement frequency matter in real-world use. A study on prolonged mask use found that long-term face mask use can affect physiological and psychological problems, which reinforces the importance of comfort and practicality [N4-R1]. The CDC also says that mask use is especially helpful when respiratory viruses are causing a lot of illness in the community, when people are sick or recovering, or when individuals have risk factors for severe illness [N5-F2]. This means that mask choice is not just a technical decision: it is shaped by cost, availability, and the need for frequent replacement, especially for surgical masks that are intended to be discarded after soiling or damage [N5-F3][N4-R1]. Overall, the evidence supports a context-specific tradeoff: N95 respirators are more effective for high-risk settings, but they may be less available, more expensive, and harder to tolerate than surgical masks [N5-F2][N5-F3][N4-R1].

## 6) Practical takeaway

If your main goal is to reduce airborne bacterial pathogens, the best practical answer is:

- **Use N95 respirators when the risk is high, exposure is heavy, and fit is good.** They are more effective at capturing airborne particles and reducing leakage [N5-F3][N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-R5].
- **Use surgical masks when comfort and prolonged wear matter more.** They are easier to tolerate and may be sufficient for lower-risk, droplet-dominated settings [N5-F2][N5-F3].
- **Do not assume that surgical masks are a safe substitute for N95s in aerosol-rich or high-risk environments.** The evidence shows that surgical masks are not regulated for particulate filtration efficiency and may let significant air through [N1-R4][N5-F3].
- **Fit matters more than mask type alone.** Even a surgical mask can be protective if worn properly, but it is inherently less leak-tight than an N95 respirator [N5-F2][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5].

## Final integrated verdict

For airborne bacterial pathogens, **N95 respirators are more effective than surgical masks, especially when transmission is airborne and fit is good** [N5-F3][N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. **Surgical masks are more comfortable and easier to wear in everyday settings, but they are less effective against small airborne particles** [N5-F2][N5-F3]. If you want the strongest protection, choose an N95 respirator. If you want the most practical option for daily use, choose a surgical mask. The evidence distinguishes transmission routes by particle behavior. In this context, droplet transmission is more localized and short-range, while airborne transmission is more persistent and can spread further [N6-R4][N6-R5]. The CDC also says that mask use is especially helpful when respiratory viruses are causing a lot of illness in the community, when people are sick or recovering, or when individuals have risk factors for severe illness [N5-F2]. This means that mask choice is not just a technical decision: it is shaped by cost, availability, and the need for frequent replacement, especially for surgical masks that are intended to be discarded after soiling or damage [N5-F3][N4-R1]. Overall, the evidence supports a context-specific tradeoff: N95 respirators are more effective for high-risk settings, but they may be less available, more expensive, and harder to tolerate than surgical masks [N5-F2][N5-F3][N4-R1].

## 6) Practical takeaway

If your main goal is to reduce airborne bacterial pathogens, the best practical answer is:

- **Use N95 respirators when the risk is high, exposure is heavy, and fit is good.** They are more effective at capturing airborne particles and reducing leakage [N5-F3][N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-R5].
- **Use surgical masks when comfort and prolonged wear matter more.** They are easier to tolerate and may be sufficient for lower-risk, droplet-dominated settings [N5-F2][N5-F3].
- **Do not assume that surgical masks are a safe substitute for N95s in aerosol-rich or high-risk environments.** The evidence shows that surgical masks are not regulated for particulate filtration efficiency and may let significant air through [N1-R4][N5-F3].
- **Fit matters more than mask type alone.** Even a surgical mask can be protective if worn properly, but it is inherently less leak-tight than an N95 respirator [N5-F2][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5].

## Final integrated verdict

For airborne bacterial pathogens, **N95 respirators are more effective than surgical masks, especially when transmission is airborne and fit is good** [N5-F3][N1-F1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. **Surgical masks are more comfortable and easier to wear in everyday settings, but they are less effective against small airborne particles** [N5-F2][N5-F3]. The best choice depends on the transmission mode, the risk level, and the user’s ability to tolerate the mask over time [N6-R4][N6-R5][N5-F2]. If you want the strongest protection, choose an N95 respirator. If you want the most practical option for daily use, choose a surgical mask. In between, mask fit, comfort, and the environment all shape the real-world answer [N5-F2][N5-F3][N4-R1].
